name: PCI DSS v4.0
description: PCI DSS v4.0 defines twelve requirements for protecting account data, published by the PCI Security Standards Council and enforced through acquiring banks and card brands. Depending on transaction volume, an organization validates compliance through an annual Report on Compliance (ROC) by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) or a Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ). Version 4.0 strengthened authentication, e-commerce skimming defenses and risk-based flexibility through targeted risk analyses and the Customized Approach, with a number of future-dated requirements becoming mandatory on 31 March 2025.
tagline: The global security standard any organization that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data must meet, enforced by the payment card brands.
auditFocus: Accuracy of cardholder data environment (CDE) scoping and network segmentation validation
Complete, current cardholder data flows and an inventory of where account data is stored, processed or transmitted
Minimization of stored account data and prohibition of sensitive authentication data after authorization
Correct application of v4.0 authentication requirements, especially MFA under Req 8.4
E-commerce payment page protections: script management (Req 6.4.3) and change/tamper detection (Req 11.6.1)
Assessment mechanics: QSA fieldwork, ASV scans, penetration testing, and ROC vs SAQ reporting obligations

phases.name: Phase 1 — Scoping, Data Flows & Assessment Preparation
phases.objective: Establish an accurate CDE scope and segmentation strategy, document cardholder data flows, determine the correct validation instrument (ROC vs SAQ), and prepare the organization for QSA fieldwork including ASV scan and penetration test scheduling.

questions.controlRef: Req 12.5.2 — PCI DSS scope documentation
questions.question: Walk me through how you determined and documented your PCI DSS scope: which systems, networks, people and processes store, process, transmit or can impact the security of cardholder data?
questions.whyItMatters: Everything in a PCI assessment hangs on scope accuracy. Under-scoping is the single most common and most dangerous failure — unassessed systems handling cardholder data create both breach risk and compliance invalidity.
evidence: Data discovery/scan results used to validate scope
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows scope documented and confirmed at least annually, an inventory of all in-scope system components, and active validation (data discovery scans, traffic analysis) proving cardholder data has not crept outside the defined CDE.
probes: When did you last run a data discovery scan for PAN outside the CDE, and what did it find?
Which systems were newly brought into scope this year, and how did you detect them?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS Scope Guidance / Req 11.4.5 — Segmentation
questions.question: Do you use network segmentation to reduce scope, and if so how is the segmentation implemented and how is its effectiveness validated?
questions.whyItMatters: Segmentation can dramatically shrink the assessment footprint, but only if it genuinely isolates the CDE. v4.0 requires penetration testing of segmentation controls (Req 11.4.5) at least annually and after changes — paper segmentation does not count.
evidence: Ruleset documentation showing deny-all between CDE and out-of-scope networks
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows enforced technical isolation (not just VLAN labels), annual segmentation penetration testing proving out-of-scope systems cannot reach the CDE, and re-testing after significant changes.
probes: Show me the last segmentation test — did any out-of-scope path into the CDE exist?
What happens to scope if segmentation testing fails?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS Scope — Account data flows / Req 3.2.1
questions.question: Show me your current cardholder data flow diagrams: where does account data enter, where is it stored, processed and transmitted, which systems and third parties touch it, and how are the diagrams kept accurate?
questions.whyItMatters: Data flow diagrams are the scoping evidence a QSA tests first. Undocumented flows (support tooling, analytics exports, log aggregation, backups) are where cardholder data escapes the CDE unnoticed.
evidence: Change process that triggers diagram updates
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer presents current, dated diagrams covering all acceptance channels (web, POS, phone, mobile) and every storage/processing point, including support and logging systems, with a documented trigger to update them when systems change.
probes: Could card numbers appear in application logs or customer support tickets?
Which flows changed since these diagrams were last dated?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS Validation — ROC vs SAQ determination
questions.question: Are you required to validate via a QSA-led Report on Compliance or a Self-Assessment Questionnaire, which SAQ type applies if self-assessing, and who confirmed this with your acquirer or the card brands?
questions.whyItMatters: Validation level depends on merchant/service-provider level and acceptance channels. Choosing the wrong SAQ (e.g. SAQ A while your site hosts the payment page) is a common and serious misrepresentation discovered only after a breach.
evidence: Selected SAQ type with eligibility rationale
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a documented level determination confirmed with the acquirer, the correct SAQ variant matched to actual acceptance channels (e.g. SAQ A-EP for e-commerce redirect/iframe with site scripts, not SAQ A), and an executive attestation owner.
probes: Does your website host any script that affects the payment page? If yes, why are you on SAQ A?
Has your transaction volume crossed a level threshold this year?

questions.controlRef: PCI SSC QSA Program / AT-C style engagement scoping
questions.question: If you engage a QSA: how was the QSA firm selected, how is the assessment scope agreed in writing, and how do you manage evidence requests, interviews and the fieldwork calendar?
questions.whyItMatters: The QSA relationship determines assessment quality and cost. Disagreements mid-fieldwork about scope or evidence cause delays, gaps, and unplanned findings.
evidence: QSA engagement letter with agreed scope
Prior QSA findings and remediation records
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a written scope agreed before fieldwork, a single point of contact managing evidence with deadlines, and evidence of internal pre-assessment (mock/gap review) so fieldwork validates rather than discovers.
probes: What did your last assessment's findings list look like, and is everything remediated?
How do you ensure evidence given to the QSA covers the full assessment period, not just recent weeks?

questions.controlRef: Req 11.3.2 — External vulnerability scans by an ASV
questions.question: How are quarterly external vulnerability scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor arranged, and what is your process when a scan fails?
questions.whyItMatters: Passing quarterly ASV scans are a mandatory, externally-visible validation artifact. Failed scans with unresolved high-severity findings block attestation and signal internet-facing hygiene problems.
evidence: ASV scan reports for the last four quarters
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows four consecutive quarters of passing scans covering all internet-facing CDE components, a documented fix-and-rescan cycle for failures, and processes ensuring new external IPs get added to scan scope.
probes: Have any quarters been missed or failed in the last year? Why?
How are newly provisioned internet-facing assets added to ASV scope?

questions.controlRef: Req 11.4.1 / 11.4.2 — Penetration testing program
questions.question: What is your penetration testing methodology and schedule — internal and external testing of the CDE perimeter and critical systems at least annually and after significant changes?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 11.4 mandates documented methodology, defined coverage, annual testing and retesting of exploitable findings. A checkbox pentest with no remediation retest does not meet the requirement.
evidence: Latest internal and external pentest reports
Definition of significant changes triggering retests
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows industry-accepted methodology (e.g. NIST SP 800-115), coverage of the CDE perimeter and critical internal systems, testing after significant changes, and verified remediation of exploitable vulnerabilities found.
probes: What significant changes occurred since the last pentest, and did they trigger one?
Show me retest evidence for the critical findings from the last report.

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS v4.0 transition / Future-dated requirements
questions.question: How are you tracking the v4.0 requirements that were best practices until 31 March 2025 (e.g. MFA expansion, payment page protections, targeted risk analyses) — are they all now implemented and evidenced?
questions.whyItMatters: Organizations assessed against v3.2.1 habits routinely miss future-dated v4.0 items now in force. Assessors must test them as full requirements; absence is a compliance failure, not a roadmap item.
evidence: v4.0 gap assessment against future-dated requirements
Implementation evidence for each former future-dated item
Transition project plan with closure status
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer includes a completed gap analysis for every previously future-dated requirement (8.3.6, 8.4.x, 6.4.3, 11.6.1, targeted risk analyses, 3.3.1.1 hashing of PAN where used, etc.) with implementation and operating evidence.
probes: Which former future-dated requirement was hardest to implement, and what evidence proves it operates?
Are any still in progress? What is the compliance impact?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.8.1 / 12.8.2 / 12.8.5 — Third-party service providers
questions.question: Which third-party service providers (processors, gateways, hosting, tokenization providers) can impact cardholder data security, how is their PCI compliance verified, and is responsibility for each requirement documented?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.8 requires maintaining TPSP inventories, written agreements acknowledging PCI responsibility, due diligence, and an annual compliance status review. Outsourcing processing does not outsource accountability.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows current AOCs collected annually from every TPSP touching account data, contracts with PCI responsibility language, and a requirement-by-requirement responsibility matrix the QSA can test against.
probes: Which TPSP's AOC is expired right now?
If your processor is breached, which requirements remain your responsibility?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS v4.0 Customized Approach — decision and documentation
questions.question: Have you implemented any requirement via the Customized Approach rather than the defined approach, and if so how is the customized control documented, risk-assessed and validated?
questions.whyItMatters: v4.0's Customized Approach allows alternative controls meeting the requirement's objective, but demands a documented targeted risk analysis, controls matrix, and testing evidence in the ROC (Appendix D/E). Casual 'equivalent controls' without documentation fail.
evidence: Targeted risk analysis for the customized control
Testing evidence for the customized control
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows the Customized Approach used deliberately and sparingly, with a controls matrix proving the objective is met, a targeted risk analysis, and QSA validation documented in the ROC — not informal compensating-control habits from v3.2.1.
probes: Which requirements are customized, and how does the QSA test them?
What is the migration plan if the customized control cannot be validated?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS v4.0 Targeted Risk Analysis (e.g. Req 5.2.3.1, 10.4.1.1, 11.3.1.1)
questions.question: Where v4.0 lets you define control frequencies via a targeted risk analysis (TRA), what TRAs have you performed, how are they documented, and when are they reviewed?
questions.whyItMatters: TRAs replaced some fixed frequencies with entity-defined ones — but only with a documented analysis using the PCI SSC template, reviewed at least annually. Choosing a frequency without a TRA is non-compliance.
evidence: Link from each TRA to the requirement frequency it governs
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer lists every requirement where the entity set its own frequency, each backed by a documented TRA using the PCI SSC template, approved by management, and reviewed at least annually or after relevant changes.
probes: Show me the TRA governing your log review frequency.
Have any TRA conclusions changed on annual review?

phases.name: Phase 2 — Build & Protect: Network Security, Secure Configuration, Stored Data, Transmission, Malware & Secure Software (Req 1–6)
phases.objective: Test the technical safeguards that build and maintain a secure CDE: network security controls, hardened configurations, protection of stored account data, encryption of transmission, anti-malware defenses, and secure software development including e-commerce payment page script controls.

questions.controlRef: Req 1.2 / 1.3 — Network security controls and CDE access restriction
questions.question: How are network security controls (firewalls, cloud security groups) configured to restrict inbound and outbound traffic to and from the CDE to only what is necessary, and how are rules reviewed?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 1.2-1.3 require traffic to the CDE be restricted to necessary communications. Overly permissive rules and unrestricted outbound traffic are leading causes of CDE compromise and assessment findings.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows deny-by-default posture, every permit rule carrying a business justification, documented ruleset reviews at least every six months with removals, and outbound traffic from the CDE restricted to what is needed.
probes: Show me rules with 'any' in source or destination and justify each.
What was removed in the last ruleset review?

questions.controlRef: Req 1.4 / 1.5 — Network connections between trusted and untrusted, and computing device risks
questions.question: How are connections between untrusted networks (including the internet and third parties) and the CDE controlled, and what protections apply to mobile/remote computing devices used to access the CDE?
questions.whyItMatters: Untrusted-to-CDE connections are the primary attack path. v4.0 explicitly addresses risks from computing devices (laptops, phones) used to connect to the CDE, which historically sat outside PCI thinking.
evidence: Endpoint controls for devices accessing the CDE
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a proper DMZ, no direct internet-to-CDE-internal paths, all third-party connections inventoried and justified, and hardened, monitored endpoints for any device used to administer or access the CDE.
probes: Which third parties have persistent connectivity into the CDE?
Can an admin access the CDE from an unmanaged personal device?

questions.controlRef: Req 2.2 — System configuration standards and hardening
questions.question: What configuration standards harden in-scope systems, how are vendor defaults removed, and how do you verify systems remain hardened over time?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 2.2 requires configuration standards consistent with industry hardening (CIS, NIST, ISO). Default credentials and unnecessary services remain among the most exploited weaknesses in cardholder breaches.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows documented standards per platform, enforced via images or configuration management, verified by periodic configuration scanning, and evidence no vendor defaults (accounts, passwords, community strings) remain.
probes: Show me configuration compliance rates for in-scope systems.
How do you detect drift from the hardened baseline?

questions.controlRef: Req 2.2.5 / 2.2.7 — Insecure services and non-console admin access encryption
questions.question: How are insecure services, protocols and daemons controlled, and is all non-console administrative access to in-scope systems encrypted with strong cryptography?
questions.whyItMatters: Telnet, FTP, HTTP admin panels and unencrypted management protocols expose credentials and session data crossing the network. QSAs verify configurations directly, not just policy statements.
evidence: Admin access method configuration (SSH, TLS, VPN)
Documentation of any approved insecure protocol with mitigation
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows only secure protocols in use, documented justification and compensating protection for any legacy insecure service, and non-console admin access exclusively over SSH/TLS/VPN with strong cryptography.
probes: Are there any Telnet/FTP/HTTP listeners on in-scope systems? Why?
How is admin access to network devices performed and encrypted?

questions.controlRef: Req 3.2 / 3.3.1 — Account data storage minimization and SAD prohibition
questions.question: What account data do you store, how is retention minimized and securely deleted, and can you demonstrate sensitive authentication data (full track, CVV/CVC, PIN) is never stored after authorization — even temporarily?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 3.3.1's prohibition on post-authorization SAD storage is absolute and is the first thing forensic investigators and QSAs hunt for. SAD found in logs, databases or files is an immediate compliance failure and breach amplifier.
evidence: Data retention policy and disposal records
Data discovery scan results for PAN/SAD
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows retention limited to defined business need with executed disposal, recurring discovery scans across databases, logs, file shares and backups proving no SAD persists, and remediation history for anything found.
probes: Run a discovery pattern against your logs now — could CVV values appear?
Where has cardholder data been found unexpectedly in the past, and what changed?

questions.controlRef: Req 3.4.1 / 3.5.1 — PAN rendering unreadable
questions.question: Wherever PAN is stored, how is it rendered unreadable — truncation, tokenization, one-way hashes with keyed HMAC, or strong cryptography — and how do you prove it everywhere PAN exists?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 3.4-3.5 define acceptable PAN protection. Weak hashing (unsalted MD5/SHA), homemade tokenization, or a single overlooked storage location (analytics replica, old backup) invalidates the control.
evidence: PAN protection method documentation per data store
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer documents the protection method for every storage location, uses approved approaches (strong cryptography with sound key management, PCI-listed tokenization, or compliant hashing with HMAC), and evidences PAN displayed only masked except for documented need.
probes: List every place PAN is stored and the protection on each — any gaps?
Is your tokenization provider's environment in your assessment scope?

questions.controlRef: Req 3.6 / 3.7 — Cryptographic key management
questions.question: Walk me through cryptographic key management for keys protecting cardholder data: generation, distribution, storage, rotation, retirement, and split knowledge/dual control for key components.
questions.whyItMatters: Encryption is only as strong as key management. Keys in code repositories, alongside encrypted data, or never rotated give a false sense of compliance and are prime QSA inspection targets.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows keys generated securely, stored separately from encrypted data (ideally HSM/KMS), rotated on documented schedules, retired/destroyed at end of life, with split knowledge and dual control for manual key operations.
probes: Where exactly do encryption keys live, and who can access them?
When were data-encrypting keys last rotated, and how was re-encryption handled?

questions.controlRef: Req 4.2.1 / 4.2.2 — Protection of account data in transmission
questions.question: How is account data protected when transmitted over open or public networks — strong cryptography protocols and trusted certificates — and what prevents PAN from being sent via end-user messaging (email, chat, SMS)?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 4.2 mandates strong transmission encryption and explicitly prohibits unprotected PAN over end-user messaging technologies. Legacy TLS and card numbers in support emails are classic findings.
evidence: DLP/email filtering rules for PAN patterns
Staff guidance and training on messaging prohibitions
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows TLS 1.2+ with trusted certificates and no fallback to weak protocols, plus enforced technical and procedural controls preventing PAN transmission via email/chat/SMS — with DLP evidence rather than just policy.
probes: What TLS versions does your payment endpoint negotiate?
Show me a DLP detection event for card data in email — what happened?

questions.controlRef: Req 5.2 / 5.3 — Anti-malware deployment and operation
questions.question: How are in-scope systems protected from malicious software — deployed anti-malware on all applicable systems, kept current, actively running, generating logs, and not disabled without authorization?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 5 requires anti-malware that is current, running, and auditable. Solutions users can disable, or systems exempted informally, leave the CDE exposed and fail testing.
evidence: Approval records for any temporary disabling
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows verified coverage of all in-scope systems (with documented risk-based justification for exemptions, e.g. mainframes), automatic updates, centralized alerting, and management authorization plus monitoring for any disabling.
probes: Which in-scope systems have no anti-malware, and where is the documented justification?
Show me the last malware detection and its handling.

questions.controlRef: Req 5.4.1 — Anti-phishing protections
questions.question: What technical and procedural controls protect personnel against phishing — since phishing is the leading initial access path into environments that ultimately reach the CDE?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 5.4.1 (new in v4.0) explicitly requires processes and mechanisms to detect and protect personnel against phishing attacks. Assessors now test this as a formal requirement, not a best practice.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer combines technical filtering (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, link/attachment protection), a reporting button/process with tracked response, simulations with remedial training, and escalation paths into incident response.
probes: What is your phishing simulation click rate trend?
Walk me through handling of the last reported phishing email that got clicked.

questions.controlRef: Req 6.2 / 6.3 / 6.5 — Secure development, vulnerability handling and change control
questions.question: How is software developed securely and changes controlled — SDLC practices, code review, vulnerability identification and patching by risk ranking, and separation of development/test from production with no live PAN in test?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 6 spans the secure software lifecycle. Common failures: unpatched critical components, developers with uncontrolled production push rights, and real cardholder data in test environments (explicitly prohibited by Req 6.4.1).
evidence: Code review records for sampled changes
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows security embedded in the SDLC, mandatory peer review, critical security patches within one month (Req 6.3.3), strict environment separation, and proof no live PAN exists in test/development.
probes: Show me patch timelines for the last critical vulnerability in an in-scope component.
Scan your test environment for PAN patterns — what would you find?

questions.controlRef: Req 6.4.3 — Payment page script management (e-commerce)
questions.question: For e-commerce: how are all scripts on payment pages managed — an authorized inventory, documented justification per script, integrity assurance, and a method to detect and respond to unauthorized script changes?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 6.4.3 targets Magecart-style skimming, the dominant e-commerce card theft vector. Most merchants cannot enumerate the scripts running on their payment pages — exactly what attackers exploit via third-party tag compromise.
evidence: Script inventory with authorization and business justification
Change authorization workflow for payment page scripts
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a maintained inventory of every script on payment pages with written justification and authorization, integrity controls (SRI hashes, CSP allow-lists), and governance over marketing/tag tools that inject scripts — paired with Req 11.6.1 detection.
probes: List every third-party script executing on your payment page right now.
What happens if a tag manager pushes a new script without security review?

phases.name: Phase 3 — Access Control, Authentication, Physical Security, Logging & Security Testing (Req 7–11)
phases.objective: Test restriction of access by business need-to-know, identification and authentication including v4.0 MFA requirements, physical access controls, comprehensive logging and monitoring, and the ongoing security testing program.

questions.controlRef: Req 7.2 — Access control model and need-to-know
questions.question: How is access to the CDE and account data restricted to need-to-know — an access control model with least privilege and deny-all default, role definitions, and periodic review of privileges?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 7 requires access be granted strictly by job need with deny-all as default. Over-privileged accounts and unreviewed access are consistently implicated in cardholder data breaches.
evidence: Access control policy and role definitions
Access grants tied to documented approvals
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a documented access control system (RBAC or equivalent) set to deny-all by default, access assignments traceable to approved job needs, and periodic reviews with evidenced revocations.
probes: Show me a role definition and three users in it — do their duties match?
When did a review last result in access being removed?

questions.controlRef: Req 8.2 — User identification and account lifecycle management
questions.question: How are users uniquely identified and accounts managed through their lifecycle — no shared/generic accounts, controlled service/application accounts, and timely deactivation of terminated or inactive users?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 8.2 requires unique IDs and full account lifecycle control so actions are attributable. Shared accounts and stale service accounts defeat accountability and are standard QSA test items.
evidence: User ID listings sampled against HR records
Inactive account review and removal evidence
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows unique IDs enforced, termination-driven deprovisioning within policy timelines, inactive accounts (e.g. 90 days) disabled, and every service account owned, inventoried and reviewed with restricted interactive use.
probes: Show me all accounts not linked to an active employee.
How are service account credentials rotated and vaulted?

questions.controlRef: Req 8.3.6 — Password/passphrase complexity (v4.0)
questions.question: What authentication factor policies apply to user accounts — password length and complexity per v4.0 minimums, lockout, reuse restrictions — and where do systems that cannot meet them sit?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 8.3.6 (future-dated until March 2025) raises minimums: passwords at least 12 characters (letters and numbers) where the system supports it. Legacy applications that cannot comply need documented analysis and alternative protection.
evidence: Password policy configuration screenshots per system
List of systems unable to meet 8.3.6 with risk analysis
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows centralized enforcement of 12+ character passwords with complexity, 90-day-or-risk-based change policy, lockout after repeated failures, and a documented, risk-assessed register of systems that technically cannot comply.
probes: Which in-scope systems cannot enforce 12-character passwords, and what compensates?
How do you prevent password reuse across your last four passwords?

questions.controlRef: Req 8.4.1 / 8.4.2 / 8.4.3 — Multi-factor authentication (v4.0)
questions.question: Where is MFA enforced under v4.0: all non-console administrative access into the CDE, all access into the CDE, and all remote access that could impact the CDE — and how do you prove coverage?
questions.whyItMatters: v4.0 expanded MFA from remote access to ALL access into the CDE (8.4.2). Organizations relying on the old v3.2.1 posture are non-compliant; QSA testing samples consoles, jump hosts, and applications for bypass paths.
evidence: Coverage matrix: admin, user, remote, console/non-console
MFA logs for sampled access events
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows MFA enforced through centralized SSO across all CDE access paths, network-level enforcement for admin interfaces, a minimal documented exception list, and sampled log evidence that MFA challenges actually fire.
probes: Can any administrator reach a CDE system without MFA through any path (jump host, console, API)?
Are MFA factors independent, and can a single factor reset both?

questions.controlRef: Req 9.2 / 9.3 — Physical access controls and authorization
questions.question: How is physical access to facilities housing the CDE and cardholder data controlled and monitored — authorization, badges/keys, visitor management, and review of physical access logs?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 9.2-9.3 require physical access be authorized, monitored and reviewed. Data centers with shared tenancy, paper visitor logs never reviewed, or stale badge lists are routine physical findings.
evidence: Physical access authorization list and reviews
Badge system logs and visitor records
Deactivation records for terminated staff badges
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows role-based physical authorization with periodic review, visitors identified/escorted/logged, CCTV retained at least 90 days (unless law restricts), and badges deactivated immediately at termination.
probes: Show me physical access review evidence and removals from the period.
Who reviews visitor and badge logs, and how often?

questions.controlRef: Req 9.4 / 9.5 — Media and POI device protection
questions.question: How is media containing cardholder data secured, tracked and destroyed, and how are POI/payment capture devices protected against tampering and substitution?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 9.4-9.5 cover physical media and point-of-interaction devices. Device skimming via substitution and uncontrolled backup media are persistent, low-tech card theft vectors.
evidence: POI device inventory with serial numbers
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows media inventoried, access-controlled and destroyed with certificates, and POI devices inventoried with documented periodic inspection for tampering plus staff training to spot substitution.
probes: Show me inspection records for three sampled payment terminals.
When were backup tapes or drives last destroyed, and where is the certificate?

questions.controlRef: Req 10.2 / 10.3 — Audit log capture and protection
questions.question: Are audit logs capturing the required events (user access, actions, invalid access attempts, admin actions, log changes) across all in-scope components, time-synchronized, and protected from alteration with one-year retention?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 10.2-10.3 make logging the forensic backbone of PCI. Missing log sources, clock drift, or logs an attacker could edit make incident reconstruction impossible and are direct test items.
evidence: Log source inventory mapped to Req 10.2 events
Log retention and access restriction settings
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows every in-scope component logging the specified events to a centralized, access-restricted platform, reliable time synchronization across all systems, and retention of 12 months with 3 months immediately available.
probes: Which in-scope systems do not forward logs centrally?
Can a system administrator delete their own activity from the log store?

questions.controlRef: Req 10.4 / 10.5 — Log review and failure response
questions.question: How are logs actually reviewed — automated mechanisms, daily review of critical logs or a targeted risk analysis for other logs — and how are exceptions and logging failures responded to?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 10.4 is where most organizations fail: logs exist but nobody reviews them. v4.0 permits entity-defined frequency for some reviews only via a documented targeted risk analysis.
evidence: Daily review records/tickets for required logs
Targeted risk analysis supporting any non-daily review frequency
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows automated review mechanisms with human triage, evidenced daily handling of security-event alerts, a TRA for any reduced frequency, and documented response when logging itself fails on an in-scope system.
probes: Show me review evidence for a specific past date.
What happened the last time an in-scope system stopped sending logs?

questions.controlRef: Req 11.3.1 — Internal vulnerability scans
questions.question: How are internal vulnerability scans performed on in-scope systems — frequency, authenticated scanning, coverage of all components, and remediation of high-risk and critical findings with rescans?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 11.3.1 requires internal scans at least quarterly (or per TRA under 11.3.1.1), with high-risk vulnerabilities resolved and passing rescans. Credentialed scanning is essential — unauthenticated scans miss most patch-level findings.
evidence: Internal scan reports for the period
Remediation tickets and passing rescan evidence
TRA if scan frequency differs from quarterly
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows authenticated scans covering all in-scope systems, remediation tracked to closure with passing rescans for high-risk findings, and cadence justified by policy or a documented targeted risk analysis.
probes: Show me a vulnerability found internally that took longest to fix — why?
Is scan coverage reconciled to the in-scope asset inventory?

questions.controlRef: Req 11.5.1 / 11.5.2 — Intrusion detection and file integrity monitoring
questions.question: What intrusion-detection/prevention techniques monitor the CDE perimeter and critical points, and how are unauthorized changes to critical files detected and alerted?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 11.5 requires both network intrusion detection/prevention and change-detection on critical files. Deployed IDS with unreviewed alerts, or FIM that alerts nobody, fail the operating test.
evidence: IDS/IPS deployment architecture and rule currency
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows IDS/IPS at CDE boundaries with current signatures, FIM or equivalent change-detection on defined critical files, and alert response records demonstrating the controls operate, not merely exist.
probes: Show me a FIM alert from the period and its resolution.
When were IDS signatures/rules last updated, and who reviews alerts?

questions.controlRef: Req 11.6.1 — Payment page change and tamper detection
questions.question: For e-commerce: what mechanism detects and alerts on unauthorized modification of payment pages — HTTP headers, scripts, and page content — and who responds when it fires?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 11.6.1 (future-dated until March 2025) directly counters web skimming. Without tamper detection, a compromised third-party script can skim cards for months undetected — this requirement exists because that happened at scale.
evidence: Tamper-detection tool configuration and coverage of payment pages
Test evidence that modifications trigger alerts
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a deployed mechanism (e.g. integrity monitoring of HTTP headers/scripts/content) covering every payment page, alerting into a monitored queue with defined response ownership, and evidence it actually detects test modifications.
probes: If a script on your payment page changed tonight, who would know by morning?
Show me the last detection event or test alert and what was done.

phases.name: Phase 4 — Security Program Governance, Incident Response & Assessment Wrap-Up (Req 12 and Reporting)
phases.objective: Test the organizational security program that sustains compliance (Req 12), the incident response capability, and wrap up the assessment: consolidating findings, remediation, and completing the ROC/SAQ and Attestation of Compliance.

questions.controlRef: Req 12.1 / 12.2 — Information security policy and acceptable use
questions.question: Is there a comprehensive, current information security policy establishing security duties for all personnel, reviewed annually, with acceptable use rules for end-user technologies — and is it actually acknowledged and enforced?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.1-12.2 anchor the entire program. Policies unreviewed for years, unacknowledged by staff, or disconnected from actual practice signal a paper program that assessors see through quickly.
evidence: Information security policy with review dates
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows policies reviewed and approved at least annually, published to all personnel with tracked acknowledgements, acceptable use rules covering remote access and removable media, and visible enforcement.
probes: When was the security policy last updated, and what changed?
How would an employee know what they may do with cardholder data on a laptop?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.3.1 — Annual risk assessment
questions.question: How is the formal risk assessment for the cardholder data environment performed — threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact — and how do results drive control priorities?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.3 requires a documented risk assessment process exercised at least annually and upon significant changes. It is also the foundation for any targeted risk analyses used elsewhere in v4.0.
evidence: Risk assessment methodology and latest results
Treatment plans and accepted risks with sign-off
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a repeatable methodology producing a CDE-focused risk register, treatment decisions with owners and dates, explicit acceptance sign-off, and demonstrable influence on security investment and control selection.
probes: Show me the top three CDE risks and what is being done about each.
What significant change last triggered a reassessment?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.4 — Executive accountability for PCI DSS
questions.question: How has executive management established and communicated responsibility for PCI DSS compliance — a named executive owner, a program charter, and defined responsibilities across teams?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.4 (expanded in v4.0) requires executive management to establish responsibility for protecting cardholder data and a PCI DSS compliance program. Assessments without executive ownership stall at remediation time.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer names an accountable executive, shows a defined compliance program with assigned roles, regular reporting to leadership, and evidence executives act on compliance status (funding, prioritization, decisions).
probes: Who signs the AOC, and what do they review before signing?
What did leadership do with the last compliance status report?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.6 — Security awareness program
questions.question: How does the security awareness program ensure all personnel understand cardholder data security and their role — onboarding, annual refreshers, role-specific content, and measured effectiveness?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.6 requires awareness upon hire and at least annually. Untrained staff are the primary vector into cardholder environments; completion rates and content currency are directly testable.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows near-100% completion with onboarding and annual cycles, content covering cardholder handling and current threats (phishing, skimming), role-specific material for high-risk roles, and consequences for non-completion.
probes: Show me training completion for three sampled employees hired mid-year.
How is awareness content updated when threats change?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.7 — Personnel screening
questions.question: How are personnel with access to the CDE screened before hire — background checks within legal constraints — and how is this evidenced for sampled employees?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.7 requires screening prior to hire to reduce insider risk. Missing checks for administrators or developers with CDE access is a direct test failure.
evidence: Background check completion records (sanitized) for sampled hires
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows screening completed before access for all in-scope personnel including contractors, consistent criteria, and records retrievable for any sample the assessor selects.
probes: Show me screening evidence for a sampled administrator.
How are contractor screening standards verified when outsourcing?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.10.1 / 12.10.2 — Incident response plan and testing
questions.question: Walk me through your incident response plan for a suspected cardholder data compromise: roles, escalation, evidence preservation, payment brand/acquirer notification steps, and the plan's last test.
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.10 requires an IR plan tested at least annually, with specific procedures for responding to account data compromise including notification obligations to acquirers and card brands. In a real breach, an untested plan fails publicly.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows a plan specific to cardholder data compromise, annual testing with documented lessons, 24/7 response capability, defined evidence-preservation steps, and ready notification paths to acquirer, brands and a PCI Forensic Investigator if required.
probes: Walk me through the last tabletop — what scenario, and what did it expose?
Who calls the acquirer at hour 24 of a confirmed compromise?

questions.controlRef: Req 12.10.4 / 12.10.5 — IR training and security alert response
questions.question: How are personnel with incident response responsibilities trained, and how do monitoring alerts (from IDS, FIM, tamper detection) flow into actual incident response action?
questions.whyItMatters: Req 12.10.4-12.10.5 tie detection to response with trained responders. Alerts queuing unread or responders learning their role during a real event are the failure modes this targets.
evidence: IR training records for response team
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows designated responders trained at least annually, alerts from Req 11 controls feeding a monitored queue with triage SLAs, and sampled alert histories showing timely, documented response.
probes: Show me an alert that became a declared incident — how long did it take?
Who is the on-call responder this weekend?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS Assessment — Findings, remediation and evidence quality
questions.question: How are assessment findings and failed test items handled — remediation tracking, evidence of fixes, and retesting — so the final ROC or SAQ reflects a genuinely compliant environment?
questions.whyItMatters: The value of the assessment is in remediated findings, not the document. Findings closed on paper without evidence, or recurring across years, indicate the compliance program is cosmetic.
evidence: Findings register with owners and due dates
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows every finding tracked to evidenced closure before report finalization, QSA retesting where applicable, and analysis of recurring findings to fix root causes rather than symptoms.
probes: Which findings recurred from last year's assessment?
Show me remediation evidence for a finding closed this cycle.

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS v4.0 — Compensating controls and unmet requirements
questions.question: If any requirement cannot be met as written, how is it handled — documented compensating controls worksheet with the four constraints, or the Customized Approach — and who approves the residual risk?
questions.whyItMatters: v4.0 tightly constrains alternatives to defined requirements: compensating controls must meet the intent, be above-and-beyond other requirements, and be documented on the official worksheet; otherwise the Customized Approach applies. Informal workarounds invalidate the ROC.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows any unmet requirement formally documented with a complete compensating controls worksheet (or Customized Approach), demonstrating the four compensating control constraints, executive acceptance, and annual revalidation.
probes: Which requirements currently rely on compensating controls, and when were they last revalidated?
What is the plan to eventually meet the requirement directly?

questions.controlRef: PCI DSS — Attestation, AOC submission and maintaining compliance year-round
questions.question: Once the ROC or SAQ is complete, how is the Attestation of Compliance signed and submitted, and what keeps the environment compliant between annual assessments rather than in a yearly scramble?
questions.whyItMatters: Compliance is continuous; assessors and acquirers increasingly test whether controls operated all year. AOCs signed without an underlying compliance program create liability and set up next year's failure.
questions.guidance: A GOOD answer shows the AOC signed by an informed officer and submitted to the acquirer/brands on time, plus an operating calendar where quarterly scans, semi-annual reviews and annual tests run continuously with tracked completion.
probes: Which PCI controls demonstrably operated in every month since the last assessment?
What from this assessment changes the program next year?
